slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used in routine screening of liver health and to help diagnose or monitor liver problems, usually as part of a liver function panel. Some liver diseases raise ALT before symptoms appear, so the test may help detect them early.

Ordered when there are symptoms of liver damage (for example jaundice, dark urine or light-colored stool, abdominal swelling or pain, frequent itching) or a high risk of liver damage: family history of liver disease, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, or hepatitis or exposure to it.
ALT is usually measured together with AST in a liver function panel. Because ALT is found mostly in the liver, it checks more specifically for liver damage.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: ALT (alanine transaminase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, and its blood level is usually low. When liver cells are damaged, they release ALT into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: High: Possible causes of liver damage with a high ALT: hepatitis, infection, cirrhosis, liver cancer, other liver diseases, a lack of blood flow to the liver, certain medicines (such as cholesterol or pain medicines) and poisons.

High: Cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern: ALT and AST are raised disproportionately to alkaline phosphatase. It points to liver-cell injury; the work-up looks for viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, alcohol, medicines and other causes.
Low: Low ALT is not common and may lead to further testing. Possible causes include vitamin B6 deficiency and chronic kidney disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALT is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: A high ALT does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Age, sex, weight, certain medicines and dietary supplements, intense exercise and the phase of the menstrual cycle can affect the result.
Limitations: ALT is interpreted together with the other liver tests. It may help tell acute from chronic liver problems, but the ALT level does not reflect how much of the liver is damaged.

When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: The liver’s synthetic function (hepatocellular failure pattern) is judged not by enzymes but by proteins the liver makes: albumin and prothrombin time (PT/INR); bilirubin also reflects the liver’s clearing work. A high ALT by itself does not mean liver failure.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Part of routine screening of liver health; helps diagnose or monitor liver problems and may help diagnose other conditions. It may be ordered alone but is often part of a liver function panel.

Ordered at routine checkups, to monitor treatment of a liver problem, with symptoms of liver damage (such as jaundice, nausea, abdominal swelling or pain, dark urine), or without symptoms when liver disease risk is higher (family history, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, hepatitis or exposure to it).

Physiology: AST (aspartate aminotransferase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues. Its blood level is usually low; when the liver or other AST-containing cells are damaged, AST is released into the blood.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: High: High AST may be due to liver disease or other liver problems. Other possible causes: hepatitis, cirrhosis, mononucleosis, heart procedures or problems, pancreatitis, hemochromatosis (too much iron), deep burns, seizures, use of drugs toxic to the liver (especially alcohol) and surgery.
High: ALT is often ordered together with AST. High AST and/or ALT may mean some type of liver damage.
High: AST rising with ALT out of proportion to alkaline phosphatase indicates a cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern; if ALP predominates, a cholestatic pattern.
Low: Low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so. AST is usually ordered with other blood tests, which often require fasting for up to 12 hours.
Interferences: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Pregnancy, exercise, certain medicines, age and sex can affect the result.

Limitations: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: The De Ritis ratio is AST/ALT. Classically it is usually above 2 in alcoholic liver disease and below 1 in chronic viral hepatitis and chronic cholestasis; in non-alcoholic liver disease a ratio above 1 may suggest cirrhosis. With cirrhosis the ratio separates alcoholic from non-alcoholic causes less well. AST is also found in heart and muscle, so the ratio is meaningful only for liver conditions.

slides.title: Amylase
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood or urine (clean-catch sample or 24-hour collection); peritoneal fluid in certain cases

What it is used for: Blood or urine amylase is mainly used to diagnose pancreatic problems, including pancreatitis, and to monitor chronic pancreatitis. It may also help diagnose or monitor treatment of salivary gland disorders and certain digestive conditions.
Changes in amylase appear in blood before urine, so a urine amylase test may be done with or after a blood test.

Physiology: Amylase is an enzyme that helps digest carbohydrates; most of it is made by the pancreas and the salivary glands. A small amount in blood and urine is normal, but too much may be a sign of a disorder of the pancreas, the salivary glands or another condition.

slides.title: Amylase
bullets: High: High amylase in blood or urine may be a sign of acute pancreatitis, a blocked pancreatic duct, or a cancerous or benign pancreatic tumor. High amylase in peritoneal fluid may be a sign of acute pancreatitis, a blocked intestine or lack of blood flow to the intestines.

Low: Low amylase in blood or urine is uncommon; possible causes include chronic pancreatitis with permanent damage to the amylase-producing cells, kidney disease, cystic fibrosis, liver disease and pre-eclampsia.

slides.title: Amylase
bullets: Pre-analytics: Alcohol should be avoided for 24 hours before a blood or urine amylase test, and fasting for two hours may be requested before a blood test.

Urine is usually collected by the clean-catch method; bleeding hemorrhoids or a menstrual period should be reported before the test. A 24-hour collection may be requested because urine amylase varies through the day, and it gives more accurate information.
Interferences: Prescription and over-the-counter medicines may affect the results, so they should be reported to the provider; medicines should not be stopped unless the provider says so.

Limitations: When pancreatitis is suspected, lipase may be ordered together with amylase. Lipase tests are considered more accurate for diagnosing pancreatitis, especially when it is caused by alcohol use disorder.

slides.title: Lipase
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)

What it is used for: Used to help diagnose pancreatic diseases, especially acute pancreatitis, and to check whether their treatment is working. It may also help diagnose and monitor chronic diseases that affect the pancreas (cystic fibrosis, Crohn's disease, celiac disease) and help diagnose intestinal injury or blockage, peritonitis and pancreatic cysts.

Physiology: Lipase is a digestive enzyme that helps the body digest fats. Most of it is made in the pancreas, with some from the salivary glands and stomach; a small amount in blood is normal, but damaged pancreatic cells release larger amounts.

slides.title: Lipase
bullets: High: A very high lipase level is usually a sign of acute pancreatitis. Other possible causes of higher-than-normal levels include pancreatic diseases (such as a blocked duct or pancreatic cancer), chronic kidney disease, peptic ulcer, gallbladder disease, intestinal problems such as a blocked intestine, diabetes, salivary gland disorders and alcohol use disorder.
Low: Low lipase may be a sign of permanent damage to the pancreatic cells that make lipase, which may happen in chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis and chronic pancreatitis.

slides.title: Lipase
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fasting for 8 to 12 hours may be required before the blood test. Certain medicines and supplements can affect the result; the provider says whether any should be stopped, and they should not be stopped otherwise.

Interferences: An abnormal lipase result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Many medicines, including codeine, diuretics, certain cholesterol medicines and birth control pills, can affect lipase levels.

slides.title: Acute pancreatitis
bullets: Diagnosis is based on the medical history, a physical exam, lab and imaging tests. Tests also help find the cause (such as gallstones) and rule out similar conditions (peptic ulcer, pancreatic cancer).

slides.title: Acute pancreatitis
rows: A very high lipase level is usually a sign of acute pancreatitis.
May be ordered together with lipase when pancreatitis is suspected; high amylase may be a sign of acute pancreatitis.
Checks for high blood fats: extremely high triglycerides increase the risk of acute pancreatitis.

slides.title: Acute pancreatitis
rows: Usually a sign of acute pancreatitis; imaging and a search for the cause follow.
Possible acute pancreatitis, a blocked pancreatic duct or a pancreatic tumor.
May be the cause of pancreatitis.

slides.title: Acute pancreatitis
bullets: Lipase is considered more accurate than amylase for diagnosing pancreatitis, especially when alcohol use is the cause.

slides.title: A patient's ALT is markedly high. What does the ALT level itself tell you about how much of the liver is damaged?
options: The higher the ALT, the larger the share of the liver that has been damaged
Nothing reliable — the ALT level is not related to the extent of damage
A high ALT confirms that cirrhosis is the cause of the damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the ALT level does not reflect the extent of damage; it is interpreted together with the other liver tests.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the amount of ALT in the blood isn't related to how much the liver may be damaged; ALT is compared with the other liver tests.

slides.title: Why is ALT considered a more liver-specific marker of damage than AST?
options: ALT is found mostly in the liver, while AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues
ALT is not affected by medicines, exercise or age, so any change in it reflects the liver alone
ALT is released only when liver cancer is present, so a high ALT points to a tumor rather than other damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: AST can also rise when tissues outside the liver are damaged, whereas ALT comes mainly from the liver.

Basis: MedlinePlus: ALT is mostly found in the liver and checks more specifically for liver damage; AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues.

slides.title: A patient with no known liver disease has a high AST. Why might the AST come from outside the liver?
options: AST is made only by red blood cells, so any AST in the blood comes from them
AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues and is released when they are damaged
AST rises only when the patient has eaten before the blood draw instead of fasting as instructed
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source also lists non-liver causes of high AST, such as heart problems, deep burns, seizures and surgery.

Basis: MedlinePlus: AST is found mainly in the liver but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues; damaged AST-containing cells release it into the blood.

slides.title: How is a low AST level in the blood usually interpreted?
options: As a sign of liver failure
As proof that the sample was collected incorrectly
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source states that low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

Basis: MedlinePlus: low levels of AST in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: Pancreatitis is suspected. Which statement about amylase and lipase matches the source?
options: Amylase alone is always sufficient, so lipase does not need to be ordered
Lipase is often ordered with amylase and is considered more accurate for diagnosing pancreatitis
Urine amylase changes before blood amylase, so only a urine sample should be tested for pancreatitis
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is what the source states, especially when pancreatitis is caused by alcohol use disorder.

Basis: MedlinePlus: with suspected pancreatitis, lipase may be ordered along with amylase; lipase tests are considered more accurate for diagnosing pancreatitis.

slides.title: Why might a 24-hour urine collection be requested for amylase?
options: Because amylase cannot be measured in blood, leaving urine as the only usable sample
Because amylase appears in urine only at night, and a full-day collection is needed to include it
Urine amylase varies through the day, so a full-day collection gives more accurate information
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is how the source explains the 24-hour collection.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the amount of amylase in urine can vary throughout the day; a full day's urine gives more accurate information.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of transaminases and methods of determination?
bullets: 1. ALT and AST are enzymes that transfer an amino group from an amino acid to α-ketoglutarate (coenzyme – pyridoxal phosphate, a derivative of vitamin B6).

2. Determination: kinetic UV method (IFCC reference procedure, 37 °C) – the product formed oxidizes NADH in a reaction with an auxiliary enzyme, and the decrease in absorbance at 340 nm is measured; historical colorimetric end-point methods are poorly standardized.
3. ALT is mainly in the liver – more specific for hepatocellular injury; AST in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, erythrocytes.
4. Interpretation: very high values – acute viral/toxic/ischemic hepatitis; AST:ALT >2 – alcohol-related injury; isolated AST elevation – muscle (compare with CK) or hemolysis.
5. Preanalytics: hemolysis falsely raises AST; physical exertion, some drugs.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of amylase and cholinesterase and methods of determination?
bullets: 1. α-amylase breaks down starch; pancreatic and salivary isoenzymes; determined in serum and urine.
2. Determination: kinetic methods with a chromogenic substrate (an IFCC reference procedure at 37 °C exists); historical iodometric methods are obsolete.

3. Clinical significance: acute pancreatitis (2 of 3 criteria: abdominal pain, lipase or amylase ≥3×ULN, imaging); lipase is more specific and persists longer; amylase also rises in salivary gland diseases, macroamylasemia, renal failure.

4. Cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase) is synthesized in the liver; decrease – reduced hepatic synthetic function, organophosphate poisoning (proportional to severity), cachexia; in inherited deficiency the effect of succinylcholine is prolonged.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of amylase and cholinesterase and methods of determination?
bullets: 5. Cholinesterase activity is determined by a kinetic photometric method; together with albumin and PT/INR the result helps assess liver function, and in poisoning the severity.

slides.title: Methods of determining transaminase activity (kinetic method, end-point), their advantages and disadvantages?
bullets: 1. Kinetic (continuous) method: reaction rate is measured at several points (decrease of NADH at 340 nm) – in the substrate-saturated, linear phase; the IFCC reference procedure at 37 °C (with added pyridoxal phosphate) is the international standard.
2. Advantages of the kinetic method: high specificity and precision, linearity control (substrate depletion is detected), automation, possibility of standardization and interlaboratory comparison.
3. End-point (colorimetric) methods: cheap, simple equipment; disadvantages – linearity of the reaction cannot be controlled, underestimate at high activity, poorly standardized – historical.
4. Errors: hemolysis (AST), lipemia, need for dilution at high activity (substrate depletion), disturbance of temperature and pH.
5. Result in U/L; reference intervals depend on method and temperature.
